o: We must replace each word of `text` with any word in its synonym group (transitively connected via the pairs), producing every possible sentence, sorted lexicographically. In Example 1, "happy" connects to {happy, joy, cheerful} and "sad" to {sad, sorrow}, giving 3 × 2 = 6 sentences. Constraints are tiny: at most 10 synonym pairs and 10 words, so even exponential enumeration is fine. The only real work is grouping synonyms transitively — a simple map of word → set is not enough because equivalence chains like happy–joy–cheerful require union-find or graph traversal.
k: Equivalence is transitive: build connected components over synonym words with union-find (or DFS on a small graph).
Each text word maps to a list of candidate replacements (its component's words, or just itself if not a synonym).
Enumerate all combinations with backtracking; total outputs are bounded by the product of group sizes, tiny under these constraints.
Sort the resulting sentences once at the end instead of generating them in order.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute force with iterative merging
a.i: Keep a dictionary mapping each known synonym word to a set of all words equivalent to it. For each pair, merge the two sets and update every member's mapping. Then for each text word, collect its candidates and recursively build all sentences.
s: Build a map word -> set of equivalent words by merging sets for each pair.
Split text into words; for each word get its candidate list (the set, or [word] itself).
Backtrack over word positions, choosing one candidate per position.
Join chosen words into sentences, collect all, sort lexicographically, return.
a.t: O(P·S + W · G^W log(G^W)) where P ≤ 10 pairs, S words per pair, W ≤ 10 words, G max group size — effectively constant.
a.sp: O(S) for the synonym groups plus recursion depth O(W).

a.i: Use union-find to compute transitive equivalence classes cleanly in near-linear time. Each root owns a sorted set of its members; a text word's candidates are its component's members (or itself alone). This avoids repeated set merging and scales gracefully.
s: Map each distinct synonym word to an index; initialize parent arrays.
Union the two words of every pair.
Group indices by root into components; store each component's sorted word list.
Split text; per word, candidates = component list containing it, else [word].
Backtrack over positions building all sentences; sort and return.
a.t: O((P + W) α(P) + K log K) where K is the number of generated sentences — union-find is nearly linear, sorting output dominates.
a.sp: O(V) for the DSU and components, V = number of distinct synonym words, plus recursion depth O(W).

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 2: mention that naive per-word sets fail on transitive chains (happy–joy–cheerful), then propose union-find (or BFS/DFS on the synonym graph) plus backtracking. Approach 1 is acceptable given the tiny constraints but shows less rigor. Pitfalls: forgetting that a word may appear in multiple pairs and must share one component; including the original word as a candidate (it always is, since it belongs to its own component); empty `synonyms` should return `[text]`; sorting must be plain lexicographic string comparison of full sentences. Follow-ups: what if the number of sentences explodes — ask about streaming/lazy generation or returning a count; what if synonyms arrive online — dynamic connectivity via union-find handles that naturally.
